chapter.title: The loop: goal, think, act, check, repeat

cards.body: Picture the intern with one sticky note on the desk: *find me a plumber who can come Tuesday.* They don't do it in one move. They read the note, pick one small step, do it, look at what came back, then read the note again and ask: **am I done yet?** No? Next step. Yes? Report back. That small circle is the whole agent.
cards.simpler: Imagine a new helper with one sticky note on the desk: find me a plumber who can come Tuesday. They don't finish it in one go. They read the note, pick one small step, do it, look at what came back, then read the note again and ask **am I done yet?** If not, they take the next step. If yes, they report back. That small circle is the whole agent.

cards.prompt: Your agent gets the goal 'book a table for 4 at an Italian place near the office this Friday'. Its first search returns 6 restaurants. What happens next?

options.text: It shows you the 6 restaurants and stops
The 6 results go back to the model, which picks the next step
It books all 6, to be safe

whyNot.a: That's the chatbot from chapter 1: one answer, then stop. An agent feeds the result back in and keeps going until the goal is met.
whyNot.c: That's skipping the check step. Results always go back to the model before anything else happens, and it would pick one, not six.

cards.reteach: Every time something comes back, it goes to the model first. The model reads it, looks at the goal, and either says 'done' or picks one more step. Nothing is booked or sent without that read-and-decide moment in between.

cards.title: Goal, think, act
cards.body:
The loop has 4 parts. *Goal* is a sentence a human writes: 'find a plumber for Tuesday'. It stays fixed the whole time, like the sticky note.

*Think* is the model's turn. It reads the goal plus everything that has happened so far, and writes down one next step as a request: 'search: plumbers near Leeds'. It picks only one step, not the whole plan.

*Act* is where ordinary code takes that request and runs it. **The model never acts itself.** It asks; a plain program does the searching, reading or clicking, and brings back the result as text.
cards.simpler: The loop has four parts. The goal is one sentence a person writes: 'find a plumber for Tuesday'. It stays fixed, like the sticky note. Think is the model's turn. It reads the goal and everything so far, then writes one next step as a request: 'search: plumbers near Leeds'. Just one step. Act is where normal code runs that request. **The model never acts itself.** It only asks. Plain code does the work and returns the result as text.

cards.title: Five trips round the loop
cards.body:
Sam's agent gets: 'find a plumber who can come Tuesday, give me one name and a time.'

Trip 1. Model: search plumbers near Leeds. Code runs it, hands back 5 names.

Trip 2. Model: read reviews for the top 2. Back come 2 short summaries.

Trip 3. Model: check Tuesday on the first one's booking page. Back comes 'fully booked'.

Trip 4. Model: check the second. Back comes 'Tuesday 2pm free'.

Trip 5. Model reads that against the goal and says done: 'Patel Plumbing, Tuesday 2pm.'

Notice trip 3. The intern hit a wall and didn't sulk or guess. **It just went round again.**
cards.simpler: Sam's agent gets: 'find a plumber for Tuesday, give me one name and a time.' Trip 1: search plumbers near Leeds. Five names. Trip 2: read reviews for the top two. Two summaries. Trip 3: check Tuesday on the first one's booking page. 'Fully booked'. Trip 4: check the second. 'Tuesday 2pm free'. Trip 5: the model checks this against the goal: done. 'Patel Plumbing, Tuesday 2pm.' On trip 3 it hit a wall and didn't guess. **It just went round again.**

cards.prompt: In Sam's example, trip 3 came back 'fully booked'. When the model takes its turn at trip 4, what does it see?

options.text: The goal, every step so far with its result, and 'fully booked' at the end
A fresh start: the goal and nothing else

whyNot.a: That's the tool's output on its own. The model gets the goal and the whole trail too, or it couldn't know it has already tried the first plumber.
whyNot.c: That's what a brand new call looks like. Inside a loop, the code hands the model the full trail each time so it can pick a step that follows on.

cards.reteach: On each think turn the model is handed one long page: the goal at the top, then every step and every result in order. It reads the whole page and writes the next step at the bottom. That is how it knows what has been tried.

cards.title: Check, repeat
cards.body:
*Check* is the moment the result lands back with the model. It reads the result against the goal and asks one question: **is the goal met?** If yes, it writes the final answer and the loop ends. If no, it goes back to think and picks another step.

*Repeat* is just the code running that cycle again. In the program it is literally a loop: call the model, run what it asked, add the result to the page, call the model again.

So the model decides when it is finished. That is why a good goal says what done looks like: 'one name and a time' is clearer than 'look into plumbers'.
cards.simpler: Check is when the result comes back. The model compares it with the goal and asks: **is the goal met?** If yes, it writes the final answer and stops. If no, it thinks again and picks another step. Repeat is the code running the cycle again: ask the model, run its step, show it the result, ask again. The model decides when it is done, so a good goal says what done looks like: 'one name and a time', not 'look into plumbers'.

cards.body: Dev gives his agent the goal 'look into plumbers in the area'. It searches, reads reviews, searches again, compares prices, reads more reviews. Twenty trips later it is still going, because nothing in the goal tells it what finished looks like. You spot this in the log: steps keep piling up and the word 'done' never appears. The fix is **a finish line in the goal**, not a smarter model.
cards.simpler: Dev gives his agent the goal 'look into plumbers in the area'. It searches, reads reviews, searches again, compares prices, reads more reviews. Twenty trips later it is still going, because nothing in the goal says what finished looks like. You can spot this in the log: the steps keep piling up and the word 'done' never shows up. The fix is **a finish line in the goal**, not a smarter model.

cards.prompt: Who decides that an agent has finished its task?

options.text: The tool, when it hands back a result
The model, each time it reads the newest result against the goal
The human, who has to watch and press stop

whyNot.a: That's the act part. A tool does one step and hands back text; it has no idea what the goal was.
whyNot.c: That's the person who wrote the goal. They can watch, but inside the loop the done or not-done call is made by the model every trip round.

cards.reteach: Think of the sticky note. After every step the intern looks at the note and decides: done, or one more step. The tool just fetches things. The human just wrote the note. The deciding happens at the model's turn.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: An agent runs a loop: it gets a goal, the model picks one step, code runs it, the result comes back, and the model checks whether the goal is met. **If not, round again; if so, it stops**, so the model is the one who decides done.
cards.simpler: An agent runs a loop. It gets a goal. The model picks one step. Code runs that step. The result comes back, and the model checks whether the goal is met. **If not, round again; if so, it stops.** That means the model is the one who decides when the job is done.

cards.body: Open ChatGPT or Claude with web search on. Ask it to find the library nearest your postcode and say if it is open now. Watch it search, read, then decide. That is one trip round the loop.
cards.simpler: Open ChatGPT or Claude with web search switched on. Ask it to find the library nearest your postcode and tell you if it is open right now. Watch what happens: it searches, reads what it found, then decides on an answer. **That is one trip round the loop**, the same one the agent runs over and over.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now draw the agent loop on paper and trace a 5-step task around it, saying what the model sees at each turn.
